thread:
Jun Park: Heads-up: ran a replay vs synthetic comparison for prefix warmup this morning. warmup curves don't line up, looks like replay yields lower initial hit-rate. posting commands + short notes. :thinking:
Maria G: Can you paste the exact commands and dataset you used? we need to be sure it's apples-to-apples.
Jun Park: Replay run:
```
replay-harness --trace /traces/prod-2026-03-10.json --speed 1x --preserve-order --kvcache=on --concurrency=200 --sample-seed=42
```
Synthetic run (same average QPS, stationary prompt mix):
```
w rk -t32 -c500 -d600s http://localhost:8080/generate -s scripts/prefix_load.lua --latency
```
Samir: Noted. did you run with the kernel-selector change from last week (opt-kernel=auto)? there was a fallback path that regressed some batched paths in 0.9.2.
Jun Park: Good call — initial replay run used the latest canary (opt-kernel=auto). I pinned kernels to stable (opt-kernel=legacy) and re-ran. differences persisted but smaller.
Jun Park: Quick numbers (hit-rate % over minutes) pinned kernels:
- Synthetic: 0m=18, 1m=45, 2m=62, 5m=74
- Replay:    0m=12, 1m=30, 2m=47, 5m=65
Key takeaway: replay's user-path diversity delays warmed prefixes, synthetic is more uniform so warms faster.
Elaine Chen: We also saw evictions during high concurrency test yesterday — logs show repeated "kv_cache: evict orphan 0x7f..." warnings. snippet: 
```
[2026-03-15T09:12:24Z] WARN kv_cache: evicting prefix id=42123 owner=worker-3 reason=orphan
[2026-03-15T09:12:25Z] WARN kv_cache: evicting prefix id=42124 owner=worker-7 reason=contention
```
Elaine Chen: Under replay the eviction churn was ~2.1x higher than synthetic for same token-throughput.
Jun Park: I instrumented prefix residency and eviction timestamp per-key and exported to perf-store. Replay shows many short-lived prefixes that never get second hits within 30s window. That explains worse hit-rate.
Arjun: For a closer apples-to-apples, try sampling the replay trace to preserve per-user session locality. replay-harness has `--sample-user-frac` — set to 0.2 to emulate concentrated users instead of uniform fan-out. Also try `--preserve-order-grouping` to keep cookies together.
Jun Park: Re-ran with `--sample-user-frac=0.2 --preserve-order-grouping`. Hit-rate moved closer: 2m=57, 5m=70.
Arjun: Another lever: batching heuristic change I pushed (short-seq-first) groups short prefixes together so KV cache lookups see more reuse per batch. On bench it improved hit-rate by ~8% and reduced token cost ~6% at similar p95 latency. (See PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/runtime/pull/762) :rocket:
perf-bot: perf/run/1808123456: replay-sampled vs synthetic - steady-state hit-rate delta: -1.9% (replay sampled), latency p95 +2.4ms, cost per-token -4.8%. artifacts: https://redwood.internal/perf/kv-warmup/1808123456
QA-bot: can we standardize a minimal bench checklist? suggestion: (1) record kernel selector, (2) preserve ordering flags, (3) same average QPS and client concurrency, (4) report prefix residency histogram, (5) eviction reasons timeline. I'll open a template.
Maria G: Agree. Also add a note to include kernel binary version and quantization profile (these change perf a lot).
Jun Park: Will add methodology doc and paste results into the dashboard. TL;DR: synthetic load is useful for regression tests, but replay (with user sampling + preserved order) is necessary for realistic warmup/eviction behavior. For investigating perf regressions we should always include a pinned-kernel run. :thumbsup:
Maria G: Thanks — can you attach the short commands + perf links into the eng-runtime benching doc? I'll finalize the checklist.
Jun Park: done. leaving the raw logs & prefix-residency export at https://s3.redwood/traces/kv-warmup/1808123456.zip (permissions: eng-runtime).
Samir: tagging runtime-oncall to watch the canary kernel revert plan.
Arjun: follow-up: I'll prototype an online sampler that adaptively keeps hot prefixes resident for longer to reduce orphan evictions. will test on dedicated pool next week.
Maria G: Great thread — thanks all. :raised_hands:
